summary: Specifies PT-TLS, a Posture Transport protocol that carries Network Endpoint Assessment message exchanges inside a TLS-protected tunnel, so device health reports are protected as they travel.

plainLanguage.summary: A health report about a computer is sealed in a locked box before being sent, so nobody can read or change it on the way.

questions: how are nea posture messages transported
how does nea posture transport work
what is the nea asokan attack
subtitle: How a device's security health report travels to the network, sealed inside a TLS tunnel.

tldr.problem: Network Endpoint Assessment (NEA) needs to carry a device's posture report (its security configuration and status) between a client and a server, and that report must be protected from eavesdroppers and tampering.
tldr.mechanism: PT-TLS runs on top of an ordinary TLS connection over TCP and wraps each NEA message in a simple type-length-value header. It adds a version handshake, optional SASL client authentication, and an error message.
tldr.outcome: It gives NEA a reliable, full-duplex, strongly protected transport for devices that already have TCP/IP access, without changing TLS itself. The IANA reserved TCP port 271 for it.

today: RFC 6876 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its TLS requirements reflect the versions of early 2013, when it described TLS 1.2 as having limited deployment.

sections.title: What PT-TLS Is For
sections.content:
The NEA architecture (RFC 5209) lets a NEA Client report its posture (the configuration and status of its hardware and software, as it relates to an organization's security policy) to a NEA Server that assesses it. A Posture Transport (PT) protocol carries the Posture Broker (PB-TNC, RFC 5793) batches, which often hold Posture Attributes (PA-TNC, RFC 5792), between the two sides.

PT-TLS is the PT binding for endpoints that already have TCP/IP access to the NEA Server, so it can assess endpoints already on the network. Endpoints without an assigned IP address yet are covered by a different protocol, PT-EAP, which this RFC only mentions.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you may join some networks, your computer has to show a health check. PT-TLS is the safe delivery truck that carries that check to the people who decide.

sections.title: Design Choices
sections.content:
The RFC lists what TCP/IP connectivity buys: full-duplex exchange (either side can start an assessment inside one connection), high bandwidth, very large Posture Attribute messages without direct fragmentation, and many roundtrips without fear of infrastructure timeouts.

Security is not invented from scratch. PT-TLS requires TLS because it is widely deployed and meets the security requirements. Messages use a type-length-value (TLV) layout to match PA-TNC and PB-TNC, so the same parsing code can be shared and the encoding stays small and easy to parse on low-powered devices.

The authors considered changing the TLS handshake itself, but chose to layer PT-TLS on top of unmodified TLS as an application protocol (using the standard application_data content type), because that needs no change to existing TLS implementations and gives the best path to rapid adoption.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of building a new lock, the designers reused a lock everybody already trusts, and just agreed on how to label the parcels.

sections.title: Roles, Port and Sessions
sections.content:
Either side may open a PT-TLS session. The party that opens it is the PT-TLS Initiator and the other is the PT-TLS Responder. The party that starts an assessment is the assessment initiator, and one session can carry many assessments, started by either party. IANA reserved TCP port 271 for "pt-tls".

The RFC advises against the NEA Server connecting to the client. A client would have to listen on an open inbound port, and acting as the TLS server it would need an X.509 certificate, which is costly to provision for many clients. So NEA Clients SHOULD connect to the server right after getting network access and keep the session open, and SHOULD support the TLS heartbeat protocol (RFC 6520) to keep it alive. Accepting inbound connections is optional (MAY).
sections.plainLanguage: It is easier for a visitor to knock on the front door and stay inside than for the host to run to every guest's house. So the computer connects to the server and keeps the line open.

sections.title: The Three Phases
sections.content:
A PT-TLS session has three phases. In TLS Setup, a TCP connection is made and a normal TLS handshake runs. The responder MUST have a trustworthy X.509 certificate; the initiator MAY also use one. The NEA Client MUST validate the server certificate under RFC 5280 and follow RFC 6125 for the server name, with wildcards forbidden in the server's DNS-ID or CN-ID. After the TLS Finished messages the session MUST NOT be renegotiated.

In PT-TLS Negotiation, which happens once at the start of the first assessment, the sides agree on a protocol version and the server may authenticate the client. No PB-TNC batches may be sent before it completes.

In Data Transport, either side may send PB-TNC batches, even several before a reply arrives; implementations MUST support this full-duplex exchange. The transport only wraps and forwards batches and is unaware of the state of the assessment.

For TLS, implementations SHOULD support TLS 1.2 and MUST support the TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA cipher suite for each TLS version they support. They SHOULD NOT include cipher suites without responder authentication, such as anonymous Diffie-Hellman, and MUST support RFC 5746.
sections.plainLanguage: First you build the locked tunnel. Then you agree on the language and show your ID if asked. Only after that do you start passing the health reports back and forth.

sections.title: The PT-TLS Message Header
sections.content:
Every message starts with a header, and multi-byte numbers are in network (big endian) byte order. Fields: a Reserved octet (0 on send, ignored on receipt); a 24-bit Message Type Vendor ID (an SMI Private Enterprise Number, 0 for IETF types, and 0xffffff reserved); a 32-bit Message Type (0xffffffff reserved); a 32-bit Message Length covering the whole message including the header, so never less than 16; and a 32-bit Message Identifier.

The identifier is a counter per sender that starts at zero and increases with each message, rolling over to zero after the 2^32nd message. Receivers MUST handle rollover without errors. The value after the header is most often a PB-TNC batch.

The IETF message types are 0 Experimental, 1 Version Request, 2 Version Response, 3 SASL Mechanisms, 4 SASL Mechanism Selection, 5 SASL Authentication Data, 6 SASL Result, 7 PB-TNC Batch and 8 PT-TLS Error. Each has rules about which phase and which party may send it; a message at the wrong time draws an Invalid Message error. An unknown type draws Type Not Supported, and implementations MUST NOT require vendor-defined types to interoperate.
sections.plainLanguage: Each parcel has a label on the front saying what kind of parcel it is, how big it is, and which number it is in the series.

sections.title: Version Negotiation and Client Authentication
sections.content:
The initiator MUST send a Version Request first, always in version 1 format, carrying Min Vers, Max Vers and Pref Vers; all three MUST be 1 for this version. The responder answers with a Version Response naming one version inside that range, or with a Version Not Supported error. Later assessments on the same session reuse the chosen version.

Client authentication uses the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL, RFC 4422). It is useful when the client was not authenticated during the TLS handshake, and the server's policy decides whether it happens. The server sends a SASL Mechanisms list; the client picks one in a SASL Mechanism Selection message (mechanism names are 1 to 20 bytes); opaque SASL Authentication Data flows both ways; and the server finishes with a SASL Result of Success (0), Failure (1), Abort (2) or Mechanism Failure (3).

All implementations MUST support the PLAIN mechanism (RFC 4616) and EXTERNAL when both sides authenticated in TLS, and MAY support GS2 (RFC 5801). The SASL service name is "nea-pt-tls". The server MUST always end the Negotiation phase by sending a SASL Mechanisms message with no mechanisms, and the client MUST NOT enter Data Transport until it arrives. Only one SASL authentication may be in progress at a time.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides first agree on which rulebook version to use. Then the server may ask the visitor to prove who they are, and finally says "all done, go ahead".

sections.title: Error Messages
sections.content:
A PT-TLS Error message holds an Error Code Vendor ID (0 for IETF codes), an Error Code and a copy of the offending message, truncated to the first 1024 bytes. The copy lets the receiver find the Message Identifier of the bad message. A receiver MUST NOT answer an error with an error, to avoid endless loops.

The IETF codes are 0 Reserved (ignore), 1 Malformed Message, 2 Version Not Supported, 3 Type Not Supported, 4 Invalid Message, 5 SASL Mechanism Error and 6 Invalid Parameter. Type Not Supported is not fatal: the message is ignored and the assessment goes on. Codes 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 are fatal, and for 2, 4, 5 and 6 the TLS session is closed. Version Not Supported errors MUST use version 1 so every party can read them.
sections.plainLanguage: If something is wrong, you send back the problem note with a photocopy of the bad parcel. You never reply to a problem note with another one, or you would be writing notes forever.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC walks through message theft, fabrication, modification and denial of service. Its answer to the first three is TLS: authentication, integrity checking and encryption. It admits that an adversary can still cause messages to be rejected by failing integrity checks, and that PT-TLS inherits denial-of-service risks from TLS, TCP and IP.

A sharper threat is the NEA Asokan attack (RFC 6813), where a healthy machine's posture is relayed through an unhealthy one. Where an External Measurement Agent is used, the tls-unique channel binding (RFC 5929) is passed up and included in the attestation, and the Posture Validator MUST fail the endpoint if the values differ. Implementers SHOULD expose tls-unique to higher layers. PT-TLS SHOULD also use its own set of trust anchor certificates.

On privacy, client authentication can reveal a username and secret, so the NEA Client MUST be able to restrict which servers receive them and SHOULD tell the user an identity was requested.
sections.plainLanguage: The locked box stops sneaks from reading or changing the report. A special secret handshake also stops a sick computer from borrowing a healthy computer's report.
